data.content_ref: inline:The problem asks what evidence within a single evaluation would distinguish a genuine reliability gain from mere checklist compliance that happens to track the right answer. SRC_001's central answer is that in the deductive case, the distinction collapses because a proof of completeness establishes that compliance IS correctness. But this rests on an equivocation: a proof that the checklist is complete proves that the checklist's output rule maps every input to the correct answer — it does not prove that a non-expert panel applying the checklist has a genuine reliability gain over an expert. A panel can be 'compliant' (ticking boxes, producing checklist-concordant answers) yet achieve its concordance through surface pattern-matching rather than faithful execution, especially when the expert's errors and the panel's checklist-tracking coincide on the evaluation distribution. The target provides no within-evaluation mechanism that separates faithful-execution compliance from coincidental checklist-tracking: its transfer_claim merely asserts that 'the proof of completeness' is the evidence, but a proof of the checklist's completeness is prior to and independent of any observed panel performance, so it cannot distinguish whether the panel's reliability on this evaluation came from genuine faithful execution or from lucky tracking on the sampled items. By collapsing the distinction only at the abstract level of the complete procedure, the target fails to identify any actual within-evaluation evidential criterion that separates genuine from coincidental compliance for the real, imperfect-execution panel the problem is about.
